newsitem.title: USA: Mars Pathfinder Mission back on track after glitch.
newsitem.headline: Mars Pathfinder Mission back on track after glitch.

text.p: The Mars Pathfinder mission got back on track on Saturday after scientists succesfully dislodged the Sojourner rover from a rock where it had become stuck, a mission scientist said.
Sojourner was wedged up against a rock dubbed "Yogi" following a fender-bender on Thursday, and had remained there because of a communications glitch.

The rover failed to receive its new instructions because mission controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory here turned on Pathfinder's receiver 11 minutes after commands were sent via the Deep Space Network.
During the fender-bender incident, the Sojourner backed into the rock too fast and one of its rear wheels rode up onto the rock's surface.
On Saturday, scientists managed to drive the Sojourner away from "Yogi" and then back up to it without incident to resume it's historic mission on the red planet.
Richard Cook, the mission manager, said the rover would spend Saturday analysing "Yogi" with its alpha proton X-ray spectrometer to determine the rock's chemical composition.

In a similar analysis earlier in the week, the Sojouner found that another rock, named "Barnacle Bill," was identical to rocks on Earth, leading scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory to the conclusion that Earth and Mars were solar twins in terms of their development.

The rover had been due to survey "Yogi" on Wednesday but that was put off because photographs taken by the Pathfinder lander showed the rock -- about four times larger than the microwave-oven-sized Sojourner -- had a dangerous overhang that could have damaged the six-wheeled-vehicle's vital solar panels, which soak up energy from the sun to keep its batteries charged.
Thursday's fender-bender further delayed the mission and Friday's communications glitch added to the problem.

But Cook said the setback was minor, explaining that the rover was capable of roving the Martian surface for several more months and that spending four or five days on one rock was "well within Sojourner's capabilities."

The rover's next target is a rock about 10 yards (metres) from "Yogi," called "Scooby Doo," which is of particular interest to scientists because it has a whitish hue; the fist ever pale-coloured rock seen on Mars.
Engineers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory hope to send the Sojouner over to "Scooby Doo" early next week after it carries out soil sampling experiments between "Yogi" and the white rock.
